A Canticle for Leibowitz plunges our world deep into a new Dark Age, traces its history as it struggles to rebuild over centuries, then, Ouroboros like, sends it back to swallow the tail of its own destruction. It is so much more than your typical post-apocalyptic tale. It is bleak, dark, and cynical, yet built on a foundation of hope. It often lampoons the structures and mindset of organized religion while maintaining absolute respect for the sincerity and simplicity of faith. It delves into matters philosophical and theological, examining thorny issues while avoiding pat answers. And it is funny — eruditely so.

The novel is actually three related novellas, each one focused on the Abby of the Albertian Order of Leibowitz in what once was the American Southwest. Each novella is separated from the last by multiple centuries, allowing a sweeping vision across time. The brothers of the Leibowitz Abby are dedicated to finding, preserving, and memorizing whatever scraps of knowledge can be salvaged from the cataclysm that wiped out the civilization that preceded them. It is the holy calling of these brothers that gives the novellas continuity, as well as clever callbacks each tale gives to long dead protagonist of the preceding story.

These separate stories are uneven. The first of the three is by far the best, where we are introduced to a simple young brother of the order during the darkest age — several hundred years removed from the nuclear destruction of our civilization. This young man and his fellow monks know next to nothing about the scraps of knowledge they are dedicated to preserving, are engulfed by superstition and ignorance, yet are fully dedicated to their holy task. This tale is simply brilliant. The next two — one set at the earliest dawning of a new age of knowledge, and the last showing a fully revived yet still deeply flawed civilization — can’t quite match it only because the bar was set so high by the original.

This story’s hook — showing the progression of a civilization rebuilding from apocalypse through the eyes of generations of sincerely dedicated monks — is brilliantly original. It should be noted that to fully appreciate the book it helps to have some basic knowledge of theology and some interest in philosophy. The author spends enough time exploring philosophical and theological questions the story raises that, if you are uninterested in these subjects you will miss much of what makes the book fascinating.

Wow. So much within these pages of speculative fiction I'm going to have trouble not only getting my head around it, but articulating any good portion of what I feel and think of it.

After the fall of the Roman Empire, Irish monks during the Dark Ages kept the flame of Western civilization alive by copying religious and classical texts. This is something of the opening premise for Miller's book. But there are big differences: nuclear holocaust was worldwide in his tale, no libraries survived, and only scraps of documents and parts of books have survived the destruction, so there is no rhyme, reason or foundation of knowledge of any real value for the next society to work from as mankind struggles to rise from the ashes.

A Jewish engineer whose few documents survived is the patron saint of a religious order built near his remains somewhere in the American southwest. The monastery scribes labor on and try to piece together his life and related work, and make surprising headway. Their repository of documents has created a reputation for their order, though they mostly just store the documents, not study them, let alone circulate them for use by others more scholarly. One of their own however, creates the "first" electric dynamo and accompanying arc light. And this is the beginning of the next ramp up to nuclear war.

The story works through three time periods at the monastery, 500 or 600 years apart. There is some comedy, but most of it is very serious.

The themes of Man's fall from grace, the pursuit of knowledge and its misuse, hope and faith in God even in the face of utter hell on earth (generations of mutations from radiation are brutally pictured), the repetition of history and our inability to learn from the past or move beyond our destructive egotism....

Miller gives us a thoughtful tract. Pessimism is very deep, for he has us taking the seeds of all our negative traits and practices to the stars with us. Some do escape the planet, and one has to wonder if that's a good thing for the rest of the universe.
